chapter_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers (Bravehearts)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Reading the Letters: Entry and First Encounter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.180): activate prior knowledge — whom should Indians pay homage to?

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading activation under “Let us read” (p.180): ask students whom every Indian should pay homage to and invite three or four spoken responses. Record key words — sacrifice, soldiers, nation — on the board as anchors for the reading.

Read Soumya’s letter aloud (pp.180–187), pausing at each Chakra description so students can visualise the four concentric circles. Invite students to follow in their textbooks and read one paragraph each in turn, keeping the pace unhurried.

Conduct a brief paired exchange: partners name one detail from the letter that surprised or moved them. Gather two or three responses aloud to the class, noting the contrast between factual information and emotional tone.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter is rich in proper nouns — Amar Chakra, Veerta Chakra, Tyag Chakra, Raksha Chakra, Param Vir Chakra — and students may stumble on pronunciation; model each name before the reading begins. A common difficulty is distinguishing the memorial’s four concentric Chakras from one another: a quick board sketch of four rings labelled with their English translations keeps the structure visible throughout the reading.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Discussing Both Letters: Heroes, Feelings, and Gratitude

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.187): war-heroes table — contribution and award for three named soldiers.
Let us discuss (p.192): why Ananda recalls ‘Pushp ki Abhilasha’ and her intended actions.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.187): complete the feelings table — find sentences evoking wonder, pride, sadness, and gratitude.

time_bands.activity: Read Ananda’s reply aloud (pp.188–192) as a class, with students following. Keep the pace steady so the emotional register of each paragraph lands before discussion begins.

Work through the war-heroes table under “Let us discuss” (p.187): draw a three-column table on the board and invite students to contribute what the text says about Captain Mahendra Nath Mulla, Lance Naik Albert Ekka, and Major Padmapani Acharya. Students copy the completed table.

Move to Ananda’s letter questions (p.192): discuss why the visit to the Bougainvillea Garden memorial reminded Ananda of ‘Pushp ki Abhilasha’, and list the six actions she plans to take. Students note answers in their exercise books.

Closing oral round: each student names one action from Ananda’s list that they would also want to take, with a brief reason. This consolidates the discussion and builds towards the speaking and writing spines.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the Param Vir Chakra (India’s highest gallantry award) with the Maha Vir Chakra; the text distinguishes them clearly and it is worth pausing on the relevant sentences. For the homework feelings table, remind students that the task asks them to locate sentences from the text rather than write their own — they should quote directly.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Gunjan’s Speech and Dreams of Service: Listen, then Speak

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.196–197): listen to Gunjan’s speech and answer five short questions in exact words.
Let us speak (p.197): paired turns — name a dream profession from the picture and give a reason.

time_bands.activity: Set the context: tell students they will hear a Grade 7 student named Gunjan explain why she wants to join the Armed Forces. Ask students to open to p.196 and read the five questions silently so they know what to listen for.

Read Gunjan’s speech aloud at a measured pace, twice. After the first reading students jot key phrases; after the second they write answers to the five questions (pp.196–197) in two or three exact words from the speech.

Review answers together: invite students to call out their responses and discuss why Gunjan values discipline, the uniform, and daily adventure. Correct where spoken wording was paraphrased rather than exact.

Move to the speaking task (p.197): working in pairs, students take turns identifying a profession from the textbook picture, stating a wish to pursue it, and giving one reason plus one preparation step. Each pair covers at least three professions; the teacher circulates and prompts quieter partners.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task explicitly asks for ‘two–three exact words’, so a common slip is students paraphrasing Gunjan’s speech rather than quoting it; emphasise before the second reading that they should listen for her precise phrasing. In the speaking activity, students from less assertive backgrounds may default to very short answers — validate brief responses first, then model how to add a preparation step to extend the turn.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Prefixes, Brave Synonyms, and Subordinating Conjunctions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.194): match prefixes to meanings and root words; complete the paragraph with new words.
Let us learn (p.195): fill missing vowels to find nine synonyms for ‘brave’.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.195): divide four sentences from the text into main clause and subordinate clause.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the prefix task (p.194): write ‘dis-’, ‘in-’, ‘im-’, ‘un-’ on the board and elicit their meanings from the words ‘disregard’, ‘inconsequential’, ‘immortal’, ‘undaunted’. Students then match the seven prefixes (re-, mal-, un-, anti-, extra-, ex-, de-) to their meanings and root words, and complete the paragraph on soldiers’ extraordinary training.

Work through the missing-vowel activity (p.195): write the nine frames on the board and invite volunteers to fill in vowels one word at a time. Discuss the nuance between ‘valiant’, ‘gallant’, ‘valour’, and ‘courageous’ briefly, using the letter texts as context.

Preview subordinating conjunctions briefly (p.195): write the four conjunctions — when, because, though, so that — on the board with one example sentence each from Soumya’s letter. Students identify which part is the main clause and which is the subordinate clause in each example. Full written practice goes to homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often add a prefix without checking the root word’s spelling changes (e.g., ‘im-’ before ‘m’ or ‘p’); draw attention to this pattern using ‘immortal’. For the missing-vowel activity, guard against students treating it as a speed contest — the goal is to recognise each word’s meaning and connect it to the text.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Combining Clauses and Reading Extracts Closely

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.196): combine five sentence pairs using subordinating conjunctions; complete eight open clause sentences.
Let us think and reflect (p.192–193): extract questions — tone, fact vs opinion, everlasting flame, and Ananda’s awareness.

time_bands.activity: Return to subordinating conjunctions (p.196): students combine the five sentence pairs in their exercise books using because, unless, when, where, or though. Review answers as a class, writing one or two combined sentences on the board and discussing why a particular conjunction fits.

Students complete the eight open-ended clause sentences (p.196) individually, then compare with a partner. Select four contrasting completions and read them aloud, noting how the meaning shifts with different main or subordinate clauses.

Shift to the extract questions under “Let us think and reflect” (p.192–193): read the two extracts aloud, then work through the tone MCQ, the fact-or-opinion question about the Amar Jawan Jyoti, the everlasting flame inference, and the question on which line shows Ananda’s prior awareness. Students write brief answers.

periods.teacher_notes: When combining sentences, students frequently insert ‘because’ where ‘when’ is needed (temporal rather than causal relationship) — address this with one focused contrast on the board. For the extract analysis, the fact-vs-opinion distinction is genuinely subtle in the phrase ‘It truly is a majestic site’; guide students to notice the evaluative adverb ‘truly’ as the signal that this is an opinion.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Writing a Letter on the Armed Forces in Peacetime

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.197–198): write a letter to a friend on Armed Forces’ peacetime contributions — calamities, infrastructure, welfare.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the writing task (p.197–198): discuss the three prompt areas — natural calamities, infrastructure development, and welfare initiatives — with two brief examples each drawn from general knowledge. Remind students of the informal letter format modelled in Soumya’s and Ananda’s letters.

Students plan their letter in bullet points: opening greeting, one paragraph per prompt area, and a closing. The teacher writes the structure skeleton on the board — date, address, salutation, body paragraphs, closing — so students can refer to it while writing.

Students write their letters independently, aiming for three body paragraphs covering all three prompt areas. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with one guiding question per area (e.g., “What did you hear about the army during the Kerala floods?”).

Paired peer response: partners exchange letters and check that all three areas are covered and that the tone is friendly but respectful. Each partner marks one strength and one suggestion. Students make a quick revision in the final minute if time allows.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have read the chapter’s two letters closely will have a strong model for tone and structure — prompt them to notice how Soumya and Ananda balance information with personal feeling, since that balance is also expected here. A common difficulty is students listing facts without connecting them to the letter recipient; encourage each paragraph to include one sentence that speaks directly to the friend.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Forces, Mottos, Women in Uniform: Exploring Beyond the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.198): read the three Armed Forces mottos; research and discuss other national forces such as CRPF.
Let us explore (p.198): class discussion on women in the Armed Forces with examples.

time_bands.activity: Read the three Armed Forces mottos (p.198) aloud and discuss their meanings in plain English — Service Before Self, Touch the Sky with Glory, Be Auspicious Unto Us Oh Varuna. Students share what each motto reveals about the spirit of that branch. Invite students to suggest other national forces they have heard of.

In small groups of three, students pool what they know about one other national force (CRPF, BSF, CISF, Coast Guard, or another) — its full name, what it protects or serves, and if they know a motto. Each group prepares two or three sentences to share. The teacher adds factual details where students’ knowledge has gaps.

Whole-class discussion on women in the Armed Forces (p.198): the teacher opens with one example — such as Flight Lieutenant Avani Chaturvedi, first Indian woman to fly a fighter jet solo — and invites students to contribute names or roles they know. Record responses on the board as a running list.

Closing reflection: each student writes one sentence in their exercise book — ‘One thing about India’s Armed Forces that I did not know before this chapter is…’ Two or three students share aloud. This consolidates the chapter’s themes of gratitude, service, and collective memory.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may confuse paramilitary forces with the main Armed Forces; a brief board distinction — Army, Navy, Air Force as the three main branches, CRPF/BSF/CISF as Central Armed Police Forces — prevents this. The discussion on women in the Armed Forces can raise strong opinions; model respectful disagreement if needed and ensure all voices, including quieter students, are heard.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and infers emotional and evaluative meaning from informational correspondence using informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two letters between Soumya and Ananda about the National War Memorial, four Chakras, Param Vir Chakra recipients, gratitude, and patriotism.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about the National War Memorial as described in Soumya’s letter. Write True or False for each statement and give a one-sentence reason drawn from the letter.
1. The National War Memorial is spread over 40 acres near India Gate in New Delhi.
2. The Tyag Chakra is the innermost circle of the memorial and contains the eternal flame.
3. The names of fallen soldiers are etched in gold on granite tablets in the Tyag Chakra.
4. The memorial was inaugurated before construction began in April 2018.

options.text: The memorial was inaugurated before construction began in April 2018.
The names of fallen soldiers are etched in gold on granite tablets in the Tyag Chakra.
The National War Memorial is spread over 40 acres near India Gate in New Delhi.
The Tyag Chakra is the innermost circle of the memorial and contains the eternal flame.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Soumya states the memorial is spread over 40 acres near India Gate.
2. False — the innermost circle with the eternal flame is the Amar Chakra, not the Tyag Chakra.
3. True — Soumya describes granite tablets etched with soldiers’ names in gold in the Tyag Chakra.
4. False — construction began in April 2018 and the memorial was inaugurated afterwards, in February 2019.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and infers emotional and evaluative meaning from informational correspondence using informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two letters between Soumya and Ananda about the National War Memorial, four Chakras, Param Vir Chakra recipients, gratitude, and patriotism.
items.item_stem: Soumya closes her letter by saying that the visit brought tears but also a resolve to live worthy of the soldiers’ sacrifice, and Ananda reflects that a war memorial is not just a monument but an expression of deep gratitude for the sovereignty soldiers protect. What does the exchange of these two letters suggest about the writers’ understanding of a citizen’s duty towards fallen soldiers? Support your answer with at least one specific detail from each letter.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The letters suggest that both Soumya and Ananda believe citizens have a duty not only to remember fallen soldiers but to actively honour them — Soumya through her emotional resolve after visiting the memorial, and Ananda through concrete plans such as creating a collage and using the National War Memorial mobile app to spread awareness.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken monologue and retrieves specific information using exact or near-exact words from the speech.
items.source_context: Gunjan’s speech on why she wishes to join the Armed Forces — discipline, uniform, daily adventure, loyalty, and duty.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the speech by Gunjan about her wish to join the Indian Armed Forces. Choose the correct answer for each question.

1. What does Gunjan say about the thought of wearing the uniform?
A. It fills her with fear and uncertainty.
B. It fills her with pride and a strong desire to serve India.
C. It reminds her of her family's military history.
D. It makes her feel superior to other students.

2. According to Gunjan, what does a disciplined life in the Armed Forces keep active?
A. Only the body.
B. Only the mind.
C. Both the mind and body.
D. The soldier’s emotions and memory.

options.label: 1A
options.text: It fills her with fear and uncertainty.

options.label: 1B
options.text: It fills her with pride and a strong desire to serve India.

options.label: 1C
options.text: It reminds her of her family’s military history.

options.label: 1D
options.text: It makes her feel superior to other students.

what_each_option_reveals.1A: Suggests the student misread the emotional register of Gunjan’s speech, confusing anticipatory nervousness with fear.
what_each_option_reveals.1C: Introduces a personal background detail not present in the speech — the student may be importing general knowledge about military families.
what_each_option_reveals.1D: Reflects a misreading of pride as arrogance; Gunjan’s speech ties pride to service, not to superiority.
what_each_option_reveals.2A: Indicates the student retained only the physical fitness strand of Gunjan’s argument and missed the explicit ‘mind’ reference.
what_each_option_reveals.2B: Mirrors the above error in reverse — student retained only the mental discipline strand.
what_each_option_reveals.2D: Introduces emotional and memory dimensions not stated in the speech; likely an inference beyond what Gunjan says.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken monologue and retrieves specific information using exact or near-exact words from the speech.
items.source_context: Gunjan’s speech on why she wishes to join the Armed Forces — discipline, uniform, daily adventure, loyalty, and duty.
items.item_stem: Gunjan gives three main reasons for wanting to join the Armed Forces: honour and protection of the nation, the disciplined lifestyle, and the daily adventure and growth it offers. In two or three sentences, explain which of these three reasons you think is the strongest argument in her speech and why, using a specific detail from what Gunjan says to support your choice.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any well-reasoned choice supported by a detail from the speech. For example: the disciplined lifestyle argument is strong because Gunjan explains concretely that discipline keeps both the mind and body active and ensures soldiers are always ready to face challenges — this is a practical, observable benefit rather than an abstract value.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student expresses a personal aspiration about a profession and justifies it with a reason and preparation step in a paired spoken exchange.
items.source_context: Paired conversation about dream professions and vocations depicted in the textbook picture, with reasons and preparation required.
items.item_stem: Think of a profession or vocation that you admire or dream of pursuing. In two or three spoken sentences, tell your partner: (a) the name of the profession, (b) one reason why you wish to pursue it, and (c) one way you would prepare yourself for it. Your partner will listen and then take a turn.

expected_elements: Names a specific profession clearly and audibly.
Gives one genuine personal reason linked to the profession.
States one concrete preparation step (study, training, skill).
Speaks in complete sentences with reasonable fluency.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student expresses a personal aspiration about a profession and justifies it with a reason and preparation step in a paired spoken exchange.
items.source_context: Paired conversation about dream professions and vocations depicted in the textbook picture, with reasons and preparation required.
items.item_stem: Soumya’s letter shows that visiting the National War Memorial made her resolve to live worthy of the soldiers’ sacrifice. Imagine you are Soumya returning from the memorial and your classmate asks: ‘Why should a student like us even think about joining the Armed Forces?’ Respond in four to five spoken sentences, giving your opinion with at least two reasons drawn from what Soumya describes in her letter.

expected_elements: Clearly states an opinion in favour of or against joining the Forces.
Uses at least one detail from Soumya’s letter (e.g., Param Vir Chakra heroes, Bhagavad Gita quote, eternal flame).
Offers a second reason that connects to personal values or civic duty.
Maintains a respectful and reasoned tone throughout the response.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student composes a structured informal letter conveying information across multiple thematic areas using writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to a friend on the Armed Forces’ peacetime roles — natural calamities, infrastructure development, and welfare initiatives.
items.item_stem: Write a short informal letter to a friend in another city. In your letter, mention TWO specific ways the Armed Forces help during natural calamities such as floods or earthquakes. Use the informal letter format you have seen in this chapter, including a date, address, salutation, and a closing.

expected_elements: Uses correct informal letter format: date, address, salutation, closing.
Mentions at least two specific peacetime calamity-relief roles of the Armed Forces.
Maintains a friendly but informative tone throughout the letter.
Writes in clear, complete sentences with minimal grammatical errors.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student composes a structured informal letter conveying information across multiple thematic areas using writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to a friend on the Armed Forces’ peacetime roles — natural calamities, infrastructure development, and welfare initiatives.
items.item_stem: Ananda plans to write about inspiring people and wants to include stories of soldiers who serve the nation even in peacetime. Write a letter from Ananda to her classmates, persuading them to contribute ideas for a collage that celebrates the Armed Forces’ peacetime contributions — covering infrastructure development (such as building bridges in remote areas) and welfare initiatives (such as medical camps or libraries). Your letter should be imaginative, use a clear informal letter format, and give at least one specific example for each of the two areas.

expected_elements: Takes on Ananda’s voice convincingly and writes to classmates, not to a generic friend.
Includes one specific infrastructure example and one specific welfare initiative example.
Uses a persuasive, enthusiastic tone consistent with Ananda’s character in the text.
Follows correct informal letter format and organises ideas into clear paragraphs.

items.source_lo: Student forms new words using prefixes and applies subordinating conjunctions to combine and extend sentences drawn from the section.
items.source_context: Prefixes (re-, mal-, un-, anti-, extra-, ex-, de-, im-, dis-, in-), synonyms for ‘brave’, and subordinating conjunctions (when, because, though, so that, unless, where) in context.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are based on ideas from the letters in this chapter. Combine each pair of sentences using a suitable subordinating conjunction from this set: because, though, when, unless, where. Write the combined sentence.

1. Major Padmapani Acharya quoted the Bhagavad Gita. He led his troops into battle.
2. Soumya was deeply moved. She had already read about the National War Memorial before her visit.
3. Ananda plans to visit the war memorial in Chandigarh. It is located in Sector 3’s Bougainvillea Garden.
4. Citizens will forget the cost of freedom. They do not pay homage to fallen soldiers.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any grammatically correct combination using an appropriate conjunction. Suggested: 1. Major Padmapani Acharya quoted the Bhagavad Gita when he led his troops into battle. 2. Though Soumya had already read about the National War Memorial before her visit, she was deeply moved. 3. Ananda plans to visit the war memorial in Chandigarh, where it is located in Sector 3’s Bougainvillea Garden. 4. Citizens will forget the cost of freedom unless they pay homage to fallen soldiers.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of the chapter’s themes through inquiry, discussion, and connection to wider civic and social contexts.
items.source_context: Armed Forces mottos, other national forces such as CRPF, and women who have served in the Armed Forces.
items.item_stem: The Indian Army’s motto is ‘Sevā Paramo Dharmaḥ’ (Service Before Self), the Indian Air Force’s motto is ‘Nabhaḥ Spr̥śaṃ Dīptam’ (Touch the Sky with Glory), and the Indian Navy’s motto is ‘Sham No Varunah’ (Be Auspicious Unto Us Oh Varuna). Write a short paragraph of four to five sentences explaining what these three mottos, taken together, suggest about the values the Indian Armed Forces consider most important for a soldier.

expected_elements: Identifies at least two values reflected across the three mottos (e.g., service, aspiration, protection).
Explains how each motto connects to a specific value rather than just translating it.
Makes a connection between the mottos and the broader theme of duty from the chapter.
Writes in a coherent paragraph with a clear concluding sentence.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of the chapter’s themes through inquiry, discussion, and connection to wider civic and social contexts.
items.source_context: Armed Forces mottos, other national forces such as CRPF, and women who have served in the Armed Forces.
items.item_stem: Ananda mentions that she and her classmates plan to create a collage of inspiring lives. Design a project plan for a class collage titled ‘Guardians of the Nation’ that celebrates both well-known soldiers and lesser-known heroes — including women who have served in the Armed Forces and members of paramilitary forces such as the CRPF. Your plan should include: (a) the types of people you would feature, (b) the sources you would use to find information, and (c) how you would present the collage to your school community.

expected_elements: Names specific categories of people to feature, including at least one woman in the Armed Forces.
Mentions at least two research sources (e.g., National War Memorial app, books, news articles).
Describes a clear presentation method suitable for a school community.
Shows awareness of the chapter’s theme of collective gratitude and civic responsibility.
